Humbly
hum'bly
adv. (in a lowly manner; the required posture of a man before God, and the manner of walking Micah names)
From Latin humilis, low, from humus, the ground — the same earth from which Adam was taken. The Hebrew adverb at Micah 6:8 is tsana, to be modest or lowly, a rare verb occurring only twice in the Old Testament.

Biblical Definition

The word stands at the summit of the prophets' summary of true religion: “He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” (Micah 6:8). Three things are required, and the third governs the other two, for justice without lowliness hardens into self-righteousness and mercy without lowliness becomes condescension. The Hebrew verb behind humbly is rare — it carries the sense of walking circumspectly, modestly, as one who knows whose company he keeps. The New Testament states the same requirement as a command with a promise attached twice over: “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up” (James 4:10), and “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6). Both make the humbling active and the exalting God's. The Reformed reading of Micah 6:8 has always refused the modern use of it as a summary of religion apart from atonement; the verse comes in the middle of a covenant lawsuit in which the LORD prosecutes His people, and the humility required is the humility of the guilty before the offended Judge who alone provides the ransom.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines humbly as in a humble manner, with modest submission, without pride or arrogance.

expand to see more

HUMBLY, adv. In a humble manner; with modest submissiveness; with humility.

2. With modest respect; without arrogance.

HUMBLE, a. Low; opposed to high or lofty.

2. Low; opposed to lofty or great; mean; not magnificent; as a humble cottage.

3. Modest; meek; submissive; opposed to proud, haughty, arrogant or assuming.

Key Scripture

Micah 6:8 — "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"

James 4:10 — "Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up."

1 Peter 5:6 — "Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:"

2 Samuel 16:4 — "Then said the king to Ziba, Behold, thine are all that pertained unto Mephibosheth. And Ziba said, I humbly beseech thee that I may find grace in thy sight, my lord, O king."

Modern Corruption

Micah 6:8 is quoted as a gospel-free ethic, and humility itself is redefined as low self-assessment rather than submission to God.

expand to see more

Micah 6:8 is the most frequently detached verse in the English Bible. Printed on banners and lifted out of its covenant lawsuit, it becomes a programme of social ethics that requires no atonement, no repentance, and no God who judges — three duties any decent man might discharge without a Saviour. Read in place, the verse is the LORD's answer to a people asking what sacrifice could possibly cover their guilt: thousands of rams, ten thousands of rivers of oil, the firstborn for their transgression. The answer is not be nicer; it is that God has already shewn what is good and their offerings were never the difficulty. To walk humbly with God is to come to Him on His terms — which the whole prophetic corpus, and Hebrews after it, says means the blood He appointed and not the blood men chose.

The second corruption redefines humility as a low opinion of oneself, a psychological state to be cultivated by self-deprecation. That is not what the word means. Humilis is low to the ground; the posture is relational, not introspective. A man may hold a very poor opinion of himself and still be unbending toward God, and men often do; the word for that is despair, not humility. James and Peter both make the movement active and directional — humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, under the mighty hand of God — and both attach the lifting up to Him, not to the exercise.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsana, to be lowly — Micah 6:8; Greek tapeinoo, to make low — James 4:10, 1 Peter 5:6; Latin humilis, from humus, ground.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsana — to be modest, to walk circumspectly; Micah 6:8, one of only two Old Testament occurrences.

Greek tapeinoo — to bring low, to humble; James 4:10 and 1 Peter 5:6, both in the imperative.

Greek tapeinophrosune — lowliness of mind; Philippians 2:3, the mind that was in Christ Jesus.

Latin humilis, from humus, the ground — the same dust of which Adam was formed.

Micah 6:8 sits inside a covenant lawsuit; the humility required is the humility of the guilty before the Judge.

Usage

"“To walk humbly with thy God” — the third requirement, which governs the first two."

"“Humble yourselves… and he shall lift you up” — the humbling is ours, the exalting His."

"Humilis, from humus: low to the ground, not low in self-esteem."
